questions.q: Checkout in Tyler's shop takes 3 seconds. Measuring shows 2.5 seconds go into one database query, while the app servers' CPU is only 20% busy. What should be the first move?
questions.hint: At the restaurant, where was the line forming: at the waiters, or at the cash counter?

options.text: Go from 4 to 8 app servers
options.why: The app servers are already mostly idle (20% CPU). More of them means more connections and queries on the database, and latency won't drop.

options.text: Look at the query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and fix the index or the size of the query
options.why: 85% of the time goes into this one place, so this is the bottleneck. Fixing it reduces total latency the most.

options.text: Double PHP-FPM's max_children
options.why: More workers means more requests running the same slow query at once, which makes the database even slower.

options.text: Add a nice loading animation to the Vue app
options.why: The wait will look prettier, but 3 seconds will still be 3 seconds.

questions.q: The team runs the query below and says, "Checkout is fast, the average is 280ms." Where is the gap in that conclusion?
questions.code:
SELECT round(avg(duration_ms)) AS avg_ms
FROM request_log
WHERE route = 'checkout';
-- avg_ms: 280
questions.hint: If 95 people are served in 10 minutes and 5 in an hour, what is the average?

options.text: The average can't tell you how many users get very slow replies; you need p95 and p99
options.why: A few requests of 4-5 seconds barely move the average. Compute p95/p99 with percentile_cont and the tail becomes visible.

options.text: They should have used max() instead of avg()
options.why: max jumps because of a single odd request (say, a one-off network blip), so it says nothing about the system's normal state.

options.text: The number is wrong because round() was used
options.why: round only trims the decimals. The problem isn't precision, it's choosing the wrong yardstick.

options.text: There is no gap: 280ms means everyone gets fast replies
options.why: With a 280ms average, p99 can still be several seconds. The average is nobody's real experience.

questions.q: Which of these statements about percentiles are correct?
questions.hint: The number after p says what percent of requests finished within that time.

options.text: p50 is the median: half the requests finish faster than this
options.why: The middle value of the sorted list is p50, and it shows the typical user's experience.

options.text: p99 = 2s means about 1 request in every 100 takes more than 2 seconds
options.why: 99% of requests finish within that time; the remaining 1% are slower still.

options.text: Averaging the p99 of three servers gives the p99 of the whole system
options.why: You can't average percentiles. Combine the requests (or histograms) of all servers first, then compute.

options.text: p99 usually sits close to the average, so you don't need to look at it
options.why: In real latency data, p99 is usually several times the average, and that is exactly why you have to look at it separately.

questions.q: An API receives 300 requests per second at 200ms average latency. PHP-FPM has max_children = 40. What will happen?
questions.hint: Little's Law: requests in flight = arrival rate × average time.

options.text: Nothing: 40 workers are enough for 300 requests per second
options.why: 300 × 0.2 = 60 requests are in flight at once, which is more than 40.

options.text: About 60 workers are needed, so requests will pile up in line and latency will keep rising
options.why: L = 300 × 0.2 = 60. With only 40 workers, the rest wait in the listen queue, so latency grows even more.

options.text: You need 300 workers, because every request needs its own worker
options.why: One worker can finish five 200ms requests in a second. You need as many workers as requests in flight at once, not as total requests.

options.text: The number of workers has nothing to do with latency
options.why: If latency doubles, the same load needs twice the workers. The W in the formula is exactly the latency.

questions.q: The dashboard shows load rising from 500 to 800 requests per second, throughput stuck at 600, and latency growing minute by minute. Which explanation is the best?
questions.hint: What is in must equal what is out, so where is the difference going?

options.text: The system's capacity is about 600 req/s; the extra 200 pile up in line every second
options.why: Throughput that stops rising marks the capacity limit. The gap between arrivals and departures accumulates in the queue, so latency never stops growing.

options.text: The monitoring tool is wrong, because load and throughput are always equal
options.why: They are equal only when healthy. Once capacity is exceeded, throughput falls behind, and that is the signature of overload.

options.text: Users' internet connections have slowed down
options.why: Then throughput wouldn't sit at a capacity-like number, and latency wouldn't grow in step with load.

options.text: Everything is fine, since throughput hasn't dropped
options.why: Even if throughput hasn't dropped, 200 requests pile up every second. Timeouts will start soon.

questions.q: Which signs say the bottleneck is in the database rather than the app servers?
questions.hint: Where a resource is full, a line forms. Where it is empty, the resource sits idle.

options.text: App server CPU is 20% busy, yet requests are slow
options.why: An idle app server is waiting for somebody else's reply, usually the database's.

options.text: In pg_stat_activity almost all connections are busy or waiting
options.why: Database connections filling up means the line is forming right there.

options.text: After adding app servers, latency got even worse
options.why: More app servers put more pressure on a stuck database. That is exactly what happens when the bottleneck is in the database.

options.text: Every app server's CPU is 95% busy and the database is nearly idle
options.why: Here the line is at the app servers. This is the one case where adding app servers is the right fix.

questions.q: Building a product page takes 20 internal service calls. Each call has a p99 latency of 1 second. Roughly what percentage of pages will have at least one call slower than 1 second?
questions.hint: Work out the chance that all 20 calls are fast, then subtract from 100%.

options.text: About 1%
options.why: 1% is the chance that one single call is slow. With 20 calls the risk grows a lot.

options.text: About 18%
options.why: The chance that all 20 are fast is 0.99 to the power of 20, about 82%. So roughly 18% of pages have at least one slow call.

options.text: About 50%
options.why: You would need around 70 calls to reach 50%. With 20 calls the risk is about 18%.

options.text: 0%, because p99 means 99% are fast
options.why: 99% fast means 1% slow, and across many calls those 1%s add up to something big.

questions.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the slow checkout query prints the plan below. What is the right fix, and what does it cost?
questions.code:
Seq Scan on stock_items  (rows=1)
  Filter: (sku = 'BR-500'::text)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 3999999
Execution Time: 2548.220 ms
questions.hint: How many rows did it throw away to return one?

options.text: Run CREATE INDEX on a busy day, so it is done quickly
options.why: The index is right, but plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes to the table while it builds. Use CONCURRENTLY in a migration.

options.text: Add an index on sku with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY; it costs some disk and a little extra work on every write
options.why: The plan reads 4 million rows to return one. An index turns that into a direct lookup. Writes get slightly slower, which is the price.

options.text: Double the database server's RAM
options.why: More memory might speed up the reading a little, but it would still read every row on every checkout. The index removes the reading.

options.text: Add LIMIT 1 to the query
options.why: The query already returns one row. Without an index the database still scans until it finds the match, on average half the table.

questions.q: In Nicole's story, why were the backups deleted along with the database being stolen?
questions.hint: Ask where the backups lived, and who could write there.

options.text: They sat on the same disk, in a folder the app's user could write to
options.why: The script ran as the app, so it could delete anything the app could. A backup that shares the machine shares the fate of the machine.

options.text: MySQL deletes the old backups whenever it is dumped
options.why: A dump never deletes anything. Someone, or some script, had to delete the files.

options.text: The backups were not compressed
options.why: Compression changes the size, not who can reach the files.

options.text: nginx removes files that are older than a week
options.why: nginx serves files. It does not clean up folders.

questions.q: Every morning at 9 a.m. a heavy sales report runs, and the shop's pages crawl until it ends. Which problem of the single box is this?
questions.hint: No break-in happened. Two jobs are competing for something.

options.text: Resource contention: the report and the web requests share the same CPU and RAM
options.why: Both run on one machine, so whatever the report takes, the web requests lose. On a separate database host, the web servers keep their CPU.

options.text: A large blast radius, because an attacker got in
options.why: Blast radius is about what one break-in reaches. Nobody broke in here.

options.text: The N+1 query problem
options.why: N+1 is many small queries from one page. Here one big job competes with other work.

options.text: Replication lag
options.why: There is no replica in this setup, so there is nothing to lag.

questions.q: What is wrong with these settings on a database host that has a public IP address?
questions.code:
# postgresql.conf
listen_addresses = '*'

# pg_hba.conf
host    all       all       0.0.0.0/0    scram-sha-256
questions.hint: Read who may connect, and from where.

options.text: It listens on every address and accepts logins from anywhere, so the whole internet can try to connect
options.why: Narrow `listen_addresses` to the private address and limit `pg_hba.conf` to one user, one database and the app subnet.

options.text: Nothing, scram-sha-256 is a strong method
options.why: A strong password check is one lock. Anyone on the internet can still knock, and bots try passwords and known bugs all day.

options.text: The password method should be `trust`
options.why: `trust` lets anyone in without a password. It makes it worse.

options.text: The database should listen on port 80
options.why: The port number is not the problem. The addresses and the allowed clients are.

questions.q: The app uses `shop_app` (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). An attacker gets a web shell on the app server. What can the shell still do?
questions.hint: Think about what the app itself can do.

options.text: Read the tables the app can read
options.why: The shell inherits the app's rights, and the app reads these tables. Least privilege shrinks damage, it does not remove it.

options.text: Delete or change rows
options.why: The app has DELETE and UPDATE, so the shell has them too. This is why the upload hole must be closed as well.

options.text: Run DROP TABLE on the orders table
options.why: shop_app was never granted DROP, so the database refuses the statement.

options.text: ALTER the table structure or read other databases
options.why: The grants cover only SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on `shop.*`. Schema changes and other databases are out of reach.

questions.q: Which change really stops an uploaded `shell.php` from running as code?
questions.hint: The fix must change what the server does with the file.

options.text: Refuse to execute `.php` inside `/uploads/` (or store uploads outside `public/`, or in object storage)
options.why: Even a file that gets through validation is only data and never runs. This closes the exact path the attacker used.

options.text: Rename the uploads folder to something secret
options.why: Hiding the name is not a lock. The attacker uploads the file and gets its URL back, or finds it in the page.

options.text: Check the file extension in JavaScript before the upload
options.why: The attacker does not use your form. Browser checks are for friendly users only.

options.text: Limit uploads to 2 MB
options.why: A web shell can be a few hundred bytes. Size limits help against floods, not against scripts.

questions.q: Which of these make a nightly backup safe from the story's attacker?
questions.hint: The attacker has the app's files and keys on the box.

options.text: Copy it to an off-box bucket with a key that only has s3:PutObject
options.why: The backup is on another machine, and the key on the box cannot delete old copies, so the attacker cannot wipe them.

options.text: Turn on versioning or Object Lock on that bucket
options.why: Even an overwritten or deleted object can be recovered, or cannot be removed at all, so the history survives.

options.text: Keep a second copy in another folder on the same disk
options.why: Same disk, same user, same intruder. Two copies on one disk are still one failure.

options.text: Zip the dump with a password stored in `.env` on the same box
options.why: The attacker reads `.env` and can still delete the file. The password protects nothing that matters.

questions.q: After the database moved to its own host (about 1 ms per query), a list page that runs 200 queries feels slower. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: Where did the extra time come from?

options.text: Load the rows in one query with a JOIN, so the network hop is paid once
options.why: Hop times 200 queries is about 200 ms. One query pays the hop once.

options.text: Move the database back onto the app server
options.why: This undoes the safety the split bought. The page, not the architecture, is wrong.

options.text: Add more app servers
options.why: More servers handle more requests at once, but each request still waits for its 200 hops.

options.text: Nothing, the network is free
options.why: The network adds latency to every query. That is the honest price of the split.

questions.q: Tyler's site runs on one server with CPU at 90%. Something has to be done by tomorrow, and there is no time to touch the code. Which is the most practical step?
questions.hint: What gives quick relief without changing code?

options.text: Make the server bigger (more CPU/RAM)
options.why: Vertical scaling doesn't change the code. It has a limit, but right now it is the easiest and cheapest path.

options.text: Start running on two servers right away
options.why: We don't yet know whether the app is stateless. If sessions or uploads are local, users get logged out and photos go missing.

options.text: Shard the database instead of adding a server
options.why: The bottleneck hasn't been measured, and sharding is the most expensive, hardest step. It is never the first move.

options.text: Do nothing and wait
options.why: CPU at 90% is the zone where latency jumps. If you wait, the site will get slow.

questions.q: After the app moved to 2 servers, some users say, "I uploaded a photo, but when I refresh the page it sometimes shows and sometimes doesn't." What is the cause?
questions.hint: Does the user decide which server each request goes to?

options.text: The photo was saved on one server's local disk; when a request goes to the other server, the file isn't there
options.why: The file exists only on the server that got the upload. When the load balancer sends the next request elsewhere, it gets a 404. Files must go to object storage.

options.text: The browser cache is stale
options.why: A browser cache behaves the same way every time for one user. Here the photo appears sometimes and not other times, which is a sign of switching servers.

options.text: The database is slow
options.why: A slow database would cause delays, not a file that is sometimes missing.

options.text: There are too few PHP-FPM workers
options.why: Too few workers makes requests slow or returns a 502. A file that "isn't there" is a different problem.

questions.q: Which of these make an app unfit for horizontal scaling?
questions.hint: Whatever you would lose by deleting any one server is stored inside the server.

options.text: Sessions stored as files in the server's /var/lib/php/sessions
options.why: Other servers can't see these sessions, and deleting the server logs everyone out.

options.text: Uploaded photos written to public/uploads
options.why: The file exists on just one server. You need storage that every server can reach.

options.text: Keeping the cache in Redis
options.why: Redis is a shared place, which is exactly what horizontal scaling wants.

options.text: Storing user data in PostgreSQL
options.why: The database is a shared store too; every server sees the same data, so there is no problem.

questions.q: In the numbers below, what is the core problem?
questions.code:
app servers      : autoscaled from 4 to 20
PHP-FPM workers  : 25 per server
Postgres         : max_connections = 200
result           : SQLSTATE[08006] too many connections
questions.hint: What is 20 x 25?

options.text: 20 x 25 = 500 connections, past the database's limit of 200; you need a connection pooler (PgBouncer)
options.why: As app servers grow, connections multiply with them. A pooler runs many clients over a few real connections.

options.text: Autoscaling has to be turned off
options.why: Autoscaling is fine; the problem is the database's connection limit. Turn it off and the app will be slow again.

options.text: Just raise Postgres max_connections to 10,000
options.why: Every connection costs the database RAM; thousands of connections make the database itself slow.

options.text: Set PHP-FPM workers to 0
options.why: With no workers, the app doesn't run at all.

questions.q: Behind PgBouncer (pool_mode = transaction) a Symfony app throws a "prepared statement does not exist" error now and then. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: The statement was prepared on one connection and run on another. How do you avoid server-side prepares?

options.text: Set PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES to true in the Doctrine dbal options
options.why: PDO then builds the query with escaped values and sends it whole, so nothing is left behind on a connection that the next transaction might not get.

options.text: Raise default_pool_size so the same connection is reused more often
options.why: More connections doesn't guarantee you land on the same one. Transaction mode hands them out per transaction.

options.text: Switch the app to talk to Postgres directly again
options.why: That works, but it throws away the pooler, and the "too many connections" problem returns.

options.text: Retry every failed query three times
options.why: A retry may land on yet another connection and fail again. The cause stays, and writes might run twice.

questions.q: The crowd for a flash sale jumps 10x at exactly 8 pm, and autoscaling is on. Which is the smartest preparation?
questions.hint: How long does a server take to start working after the crowd arrives?

options.text: Raise the minimum replicas before the sale, and keep a rate limit in place
options.why: You know the crowd in advance. Servers that are already running save you the delay of five minutes or so.

options.text: Rely entirely on autoscaling
options.why: Measuring, deciding, starting and warm-up take several minutes, and the old servers collapse in the meantime.

options.text: Set max replicas to 1000
options.why: A higher max doesn't shorten the delay in the jump; it only raises the bill and the pressure on the database.

options.text: Raise the CPU target to 90%
options.why: Scaling would start even later, and by then latency has already spiked.

questions.q: Tyler's system has 2 app servers, 1 nginx LB, 1 Postgres primary and 1 replica. Which are SPOFs?
questions.hint: The one that, when it dies, blocks the site or writes even though the rest are healthy.

options.text: The lone nginx LB
options.why: Every request goes through it, and there is no backup copy. If it dies, the site is down even though the app servers are healthy.

options.text: The Postgres primary (without automatic failover)
options.why: Even with a replica, without failover writes stop the moment the primary dies, until someone promotes the replica by hand.

options.text: Either one of the two app servers
options.why: The other serves the remaining requests. It will be slower, but not down, which is exactly why you keep several copies.

options.text: The Postgres replica
options.why: If the replica dies, read capacity drops, but reads and writes on the primary carry on.

questions.q: Most requests to an API take 10ms, but a few "download report" requests run for 30 seconds. With round robin some servers often bog down. What do you do?
questions.hint: When you count in turns, does it tell heavy work from light work?

options.text: Turn on least_conn
options.why: A server holding many long requests shows a high connection count, so the LB sends new ones elsewhere.

options.text: Double the number of servers
options.why: The problem isn't the number but the splitting rule. Even with more servers, an unlucky one can pile up heavy requests under round robin.

options.text: Turn on ip_hash
options.why: That makes the split even more uneven. It goes by IP and doesn't look at what each request does.

options.text: Keep weight=1 on every server
options.why: Equal weights mean equal counts; the weight of a long job isn't captured by that.

questions.q: You want to spread reads across database replicas (PostgreSQL, port 5432). What kind of load balancer do you need?
questions.hint: Does the database speak HTTP, or some other protocol?

options.text: L4 (TCP), such as nginx stream or HAProxy in tcp mode
options.why: PostgreSQL isn't HTTP. L4 just splits TCP connections without understanding the protocol.

options.text: L7 (HTTP), splitting by path
options.why: PostgreSQL has no URL path, so an HTTP LB can't even make sense of it.

options.text: Neither: you can't load balance a database
options.why: Spreading reads across read replicas is very common.

options.text: DNS round robin is the only way
options.why: DNS caching makes the split uneven and slow, and a dead server's address stays in the list. An L4 LB is far better.

questions.q: The team builds a health check endpoint that runs "SELECT 1 to see if the database is fine". One night the database goes 20 seconds slow. What can happen?
questions.hint: All app servers look at the same database. If the check fails, how many servers get removed?

options.text: The check fails on every app server at once and the LB removes them all: a small slowdown takes the whole site down
options.why: The database is a shared dependency, so its trouble makes every server look sick together. Removing servers doesn't add to the database's problem, but the site is completely down.

options.text: The LB removes only the slow server and everything else stays fine
options.why: The problem isn't one server, it's the shared database. All servers will fail for the same reason.

options.text: Nothing, because SELECT 1 is a very small query
options.why: When the database is slow or its connections are full, even the smallest query gets stuck or times out.

options.text: The database will speed up because the LB eases the pressure
options.why: The LB doesn't reduce the database's load. If every server is removed, users simply can't reach the site.

questions.q: Two nginx boxes share one IP via keepalived. LB A's machine stays up but its nginx crashes. What keeps the site alive?
questions.hint: The machine answers heartbeats; what tells keepalived nginx itself is dead?

options.text: A track_script that checks nginx, so A gives up the IP after repeated failures and B claims it
options.why: Heartbeats only prove the machine is alive. The script makes keepalived judge the thing that matters, nginx.

options.text: Nothing: B takes over only when the whole machine of A is down
options.why: Without a script check that is true, and the site would stay down while A keeps the IP and drops every request.

options.text: DNS automatically points visitors to B
options.why: DNS never changes here. Both boxes share one IP, and DNS caching would make a DNS switch slow anyway.

options.text: The app servers notice and restart nginx
options.why: App servers sit behind the LB and know nothing about it. The two LBs have to watch each other.

questions.q: 300 office staff visit a site that uses ip_hash, and one server is close to collapse while the others sit idle. Which are correct fixes?
questions.hint: What is the root cause: the IP, or the state inside the server?

options.text: Move sessions to Redis, remove ip_hash and use least_conn
options.why: Once the state is outside, stickiness isn't needed, and the LB can split the load truly evenly.

options.text: Use cookie-based stickiness (not IP), as a temporary measure
options.why: A cookie identifies each user separately, whereas everyone behind a NAT looks the same by IP. Still, it's only temporary relief.

options.text: Keep ip_hash and make that server bigger
options.why: The same problem returns as soon as a bigger office arrives, and if the server dies all those users lose their sessions.

options.text: Lower the weight of the other servers
options.why: That pushes even more of the crowd onto that one server. It turns the problem the wrong way round.

questions.q: A cache cluster has 4 nodes and picks the node with `crc32($key) % 4`. You add a 5th node before a sale. What do you see in the first minute?
questions.hint: Out of four keys, how many stay on their old node?

options.text: About 80% of keys move to another node, the hit rate collapses and the database gets slammed
options.why: The remainders mod 4 and mod 5 agree for only 4 out of every 20 values (20%), so the other 80% of keys are looked up on a new node and not found.

options.text: About 20% of keys move and everything else is fine
options.why: That is the result with consistent hashing. With hash % N, 80% move.

options.text: Nothing changes, the new node just sits empty
options.why: The rule depends on N, so changing N changes the result for almost every key.

options.text: All keys move, 100% of them
options.why: Nearly all move, but roughly 20% stay in their place.

questions.q: The ring has nodes A=10, B=40, C=70, D=90 (circle 0-99). A key hashes to 95. Which node does it go to?
questions.hint: Walking clockwise from 95, what do you meet?

options.text: A (10), the first node after going round the circle
options.why: There is no node after 95, so you wrap past 0 and find A at 10. This is the wrap-around.

options.text: D (90), the nearest node
options.why: The rule isn't "nearest", it's "first clockwise". 90 is behind you.
70 is far behind, against the clockwise direction.

options.text: None: the key is lost
options.why: The ring is a circle, so there is always an owner.

questions.q: Which of these statements about virtual nodes are correct?
questions.hint: In how many places does one real node sit on the ring?

options.text: One real node takes many positions on the ring
options.why: Each position is hashed separately from the node's name, such as `redis-1#0`, `redis-1#1`.

options.text: The split becomes more even
options.why: With many small slices added together, each node's share comes close to 1/N by the law of averages.

options.text: When a node dies, its keys spread across all the nodes and don't land on one neighbor
options.why: Its positions were scattered around the ring, so the next nodes clockwise belong to different real nodes.

options.text: It adds no memory or add() work at all
options.why: You must store and sort N x 150 positions; the cost is small but not zero.

questions.q: A 4-node ring (150 vnodes each) built with HashRing is running. redis-3 dies and is removed from the ring. What happens next?
questions.hint: Which keys were owned by redis-3?

options.text: Only redis-3's share, about 25% of keys, will miss; the keys of the other nodes stay where they were
options.why: On the ring only the dead node's slices go to the next node clockwise. Thanks to vnodes they spread almost evenly over the three nodes.

options.text: About 80% of keys will miss, because the number of nodes changed
options.why: 80% is the hash % N figure. On a ring the node count doesn't directly decide where keys live.

options.text: Every key is hashed again, so the whole cache is empty
options.why: A key's hash doesn't change. Only the ownership of positions changes, and only in the dead node's part.

options.text: redis-4 alone takes the whole load
options.why: Because of vnodes, redis-3's positions were spread around the whole ring, so the load is split across three nodes and not dumped on one.

questions.q: One product page key (`product:iphone`) is the most read key on sale day, and its node is at 95% CPU. What do you do?
questions.hint: A ring splits keys, but on how many nodes does a single key live?

options.text: Spread the load with a local cache of a few seconds inside the app, or by keeping several copies of the key
options.why: It is a single key, so the ring doesn't help. A local cache keeps most reads from ever reaching Redis.

options.text: Double the node's vnode count
options.why: Vnodes decide how many keys each node gets, but this key will still live on just one node.

options.text: Add more nodes
options.why: A new node takes a share of other keys, but `product:iphone` will still live on a single node.

options.text: Change the hash function from crc32 to md5
options.why: A hash function only changes where things sit on the circle. It doesn't change the fact that a key has exactly one owner.

questions.q: A 5-node etcd cluster splits into 3 and 2 nodes because of a network problem. What happens?
questions.hint: quorum = N/2 + 1. Which half has it?

options.text: The 3-node side elects a leader and accepts writes; the 2-node side can't accept writes
options.why: The 3-node side reaches the quorum (3). The 2-node side can't pass any decision, so there is no split brain.

options.text: Both sides elect their own leader and take separate writes
options.why: This is exactly what a quorum prevents. Two halves can't both be a majority.

options.text: The whole cluster shuts down
options.why: The 3-node side stays up; only the 2-node side is stalled.

options.text: The 2-node side becomes leader because the smaller side votes faster
options.why: Speed decides nothing. Becoming leader takes the votes of a quorum.

questions.q: The monthly payroll cron exists on both servers. Which measures stop the same salary from being paid twice?
questions.hint: One measure picks who does the job, another guards the final result.

options.text: Taking a lock named payroll:<month> with Symfony LockFactory
options.why: Only one can pick up the job at a time, so in the normal case the second one returns.

options.text: Inserting salary rows with a unique constraint on (employee_id, month)
options.why: Even if the lock slips, the database won't accept a second row. This is the last line of defense.

options.text: Having the cron check at the start whether today's salary has been paid, and start paying if not
options.why: That is check-then-act. Two servers look at the same moment, both see "not paid", and both pay.

options.text: Syncing the two servers' clocks and running one of them 1 second later
options.why: Clocks aren't exact, and with the delay both will still do the work. It doesn't choose a single one.

questions.q: Where is the risk in the code below?
questions.hint: The job takes 10 minutes and the lock lasts 5 seconds.

options.text: The lock expires after 5 seconds and another server starts the same export; it needs refresh() and try/finally
options.why: The ttl is far shorter than the job. Without refresh() the lock slips away by itself, and on an exception release() never runs either.

options.text: It should throw an exception when acquire() fails
options.why: Quietly returning on failure is the normal behavior; someone else doing the work isn't a problem.

options.text: Making the ttl 1 day fixes everything
options.why: If the server dies, the lock stays held for a day. A short ttl plus refresh() is the right way.

options.text: The ttl plays no role, release() protects the lock
options.why: release() only runs on normal completion; if the process dies, only the ttl frees the lock.

questions.q: The lock service gives A token 33. A goes into a 40-second GC pause, the lock expires, B gets token 34 and writes. A wakes up and tries to write with token 33. What happens in a fenced database?
questions.hint: Compare 33 with the last token the database has seen.

options.text: The database sees 33 < 34 and rejects A's write
options.why: In WHERE last_token <= :token the check 34 <= 33 fails, so nothing is updated. A learns it is no longer the leader.

options.text: A's write lands on top of B's, because A arrived later
options.why: That is what would happen without fencing. With the token check it no longer does.

options.text: The lock service blocks A's write
options.why: The lock service isn't on the write path. The blocking is the storage's job.

options.text: Both writes get merged
options.why: Nothing is merged. A write with a stale token is thrown away completely.

questions.q: The team wants a 4-node etcd cluster because it must be better than 3. What do you advise?
questions.hint: How many nodes can die in a 3-node and in a 4-node cluster?

options.text: Use 3 or 5 nodes; with 4, fault tolerance equals 3's (1 node) and it only costs more
options.why: With 4 nodes the quorum is 3, so two failures stop it. 3 nodes also tolerate exactly one, at lower cost.

options.text: 4 is better, because it works even with 2 dead
options.why: With 2 of 4 dead, the remaining 2 are below the quorum (3), and the cluster stalls.

options.text: Use 2 nodes, it is cheaper
options.why: With 2 nodes the quorum is 2, so one death stalls it, which is even worse tolerance than a single node.

options.text: The number of nodes doesn't matter at all
options.why: The quorum calculation depends directly on the count; that is what sets the fault tolerance.

questions.q: A user posts a comment and refreshes the page, but doesn't see their comment until 10 seconds later. Which solutions are right?
questions.hint: The comment is on the primary, but where is the page reading from?

options.text: After a write, serve that user's reads from the primary for a few seconds
options.why: This is read-your-writes. For the duration of the lag, they see the primary's new data.

options.text: Return the new comment in the POST response and put it straight on the page
options.why: No read from the database is needed at all, so lag never comes into it.

options.text: Add more replicas
options.why: More replicas means more copies that can fall behind. It doesn't reduce lag, and may increase it.

options.text: Read everything from the primary and shut the replicas down
options.why: It fixes the problem, but destroys the replicas' main purpose (sharing the read load). Choosing the primary for a short time is enough.

questions.q: A user refreshes and the first time sees the new post, the second time it has vanished, the third time it's back. What is the cause and the remedy?
questions.hint: Does every refresh go to the same replica?

options.text: The two replicas have different lag; pinning each user to one replica (user id hash) stops time going backwards
options.why: Reading from a different replica each time gives a new answer once and an old one next. Sending one user always to the same replica means at least they never go back further than before.

options.text: It's the browser cache; press Ctrl+F5
options.why: A browser cache shows the same answer again and again; it doesn't come and go.

options.text: The write on the primary is getting lost
options.why: If the write were lost, it would never reach any replica.

options.text: The database index is corrupted
options.why: A corrupted index would always give the wrong result, not right one time and wrong another.

questions.q: What is the problem in the code below?
questions.hint: How long will this one statement take, and what happens to everyone else meanwhile?

options.text: One giant transaction: a surge of locks and WAL, replica lag grows, a failure rolls everything back, and it can't be stopped and resumed
options.why: The right way is small batches, keyset by id, and pausing when lag is high.

options.text: No problem, the database batches it by itself
options.why: One statement is one transaction. The database doesn't break it up on its own.

options.text: It is slow only because the id column has no index
options.why: id is probably the primary key. The problem isn't an index, it's the size of the operation.

options.text: Using COPY instead of INSERT fixes everything
options.why: COPY may be faster, but the same giant transaction and the lag problem remain.

questions.q: During dual write, a write to the new place fails for a moment. What is the best behavior?
questions.hint: The user has placed an order; which place is still the source of truth?

options.text: If the old write succeeded, treat the order as successful; log the new failure and queue a repair job
options.why: The old one is still the source of truth. You must not block the user's order, and the gap can be filled later.

options.text: Roll both back and show the user an error
options.why: A problem in the new system would block the user's money transaction. It needlessly breaks the site.

options.text: Ignore the failure on the new one
options.why: The gap would never get filled, and data would be lost at cutover.

options.text: Make the new one the source of truth and throw the old one away
options.why: Verification and backfill aren't finished. Switching the source of truth in this state is a path to data loss.

questions.q: The backfill has read order #9 as "pending". The customer pays, so the old table now says "paid". Which setup keeps "paid" in the new table?
questions.hint: Who writes last, and what does the backfill's INSERT do when the row exists?

options.text: Dual write upserts into the new table, and the backfill inserts with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
options.why: If the upsert comes first, the backfill's old copy is skipped. If the backfill comes first, the upsert overwrites it with "paid". Either way "paid" wins.

options.text: Dual write only UPDATEs, and the backfill uses ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
options.why: An UPDATE finds no row if the backfill hasn't reached it, and a later DO UPDATE would overwrite "paid" with the older "pending".

options.text: Stop the site while the backfill runs
options.why: It would work, but it defeats the point of a migration with the shop open.

options.text: Run the backfill twice and keep the second result
options.why: The second run reads at some moment too, so the same race is still there.

questions.q: Before cutover, both tables have the same number of rows (1,200,000). Why must you still compare checksums?
questions.hint: If two rows have the same id, must their values be the same?

options.text: With the same count, some rows can still have different values (status, amount); a checksum catches that
options.why: Rows that changed after the backfill may be wrong because of gaps in dual write. A count doesn't see this.

options.text: A checksum is fast, so always use it instead of a count
options.why: Speed isn't the reason. A count is a cheap first check, and a checksum matches the values.

options.text: If the count matches, the checksum will never match
options.why: With correct data both match. A count alone is just not sufficient evidence.

options.text: You don't need a checksum, a shadow read is enough; they say the same thing
options.why: A shadow read only compares the rows users actually ask for; rows that were missed show up in the checksum.

questions.q: Which of these events count as a "partition"?
questions.hint: The question is: can the nodes talk to each other?

options.text: The ISP link between two data centers is cut
options.why: Both sides are alive but can't reach each other. This is the classic partition.

options.text: The leader is stuck in a 40-second GC pause and the followers have timed out
options.why: To the followers, the leader is lost. Slow and dead can't be told apart, so you handle this like a partition.

options.text: One server's disk fails and the server goes down
options.why: This is the node's own failure (a crash). The network hasn't split, and the others can still talk to each other.

options.text: A developer ran a wrong SQL statement
options.why: This is an application mistake, not a network or node problem.

questions.q: In a cinema ticket app, a network problem cuts the order server off from the seat database. The seat state can't be confirmed. What should you do?
questions.hint: What happens if one seat is sold to two people, and what happens if people wait a while?

options.text: Return 503 with Retry-After and ask the user to try later (the CP path)
options.why: Selling one seat to two people does much bigger damage, so don't sell without being sure.

options.text: Look at the old cache, treat the seat as "free" and sell it
options.why: That is the AP path. Stale information can sell the same seat to two people, which this feature can't accept.

options.text: Keep processing all orders silently and reconcile later
options.why: When you reconcile, someone has to be told "sorry, no seat", after their money was taken. The damage is larger.

options.text: Shut the whole app down
options.why: Shutting everything down is needless. Block only booking; the movie listings and the rest can keep working.

questions.q: What is wrong with this CP feature?
questions.hint: What can happen if a number like a balance is 5 minutes old?

options.text: It decides on a withdrawal from a balance that is 5 minutes old, cached from a replica; it should read from the primary
options.why: A balance is a CP feature. A stale number doesn't show money already withdrawn, so an overdraft can happen.

options.text: It should use fetchAllAssociative instead of fetchOne
options.why: It isn't a matter of the read method. The problem is where the data is read from and how stale it is.

options.text: expiresAfter(300) should be raised to get more cache hits
options.why: Older data means even more risk.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, having a cache is always good
options.why: A cache is great for an AP feature like a like count, not for money decisions.

questions.q: A withdrawal call returns 503 after a connection error. The app retries, and later the account shows two payouts. What was missing?
questions.hint: When the connection broke, did the first withdrawal happen or not?

options.text: An idempotency key, so the ledger recognizes the retry and returns the first result
options.why: A lost reply doesn't mean the write failed. With the key, a repeat is recognized and not applied again.

options.text: A longer Retry-After value
options.why: Waiting longer doesn't tell the ledger the retry is the same request. A late retry can still double-pay.

options.text: Reading the balance from a replica before retrying
options.why: A replica may not have the first withdrawal yet, so it can say "not paid" when it was.

options.text: Never retry, and show an error
options.why: Users would be stuck guessing whether the money moved. A safe retry is the better answer.

questions.q: The network is completely healthy, with no partition. Yet the database insists every write needs agreement from three regions, and writes have become slow. Which part of PACELC is this?
questions.hint: What choice does the "Else" part talk about?

options.text: The Consistency in Else: buying correctness with latency
options.why: There is no partition, yet getting everyone's agreement costs latency. That is EC.

options.text: The Availability choice in a Partition
options.why: There is no partition here, so the P part doesn't apply.

options.text: It is a CAP failure, unrelated to PACELC
options.why: CAP only speaks about the time of a partition; PACELC names exactly this choice made while "the line is fine".

options.text: A bug in the database
options.why: This is the normal price of the design, not a bug.

questions.q: In an AP-style system, the same profile bio is changed on both sides, and the system applies "last write wins" (by the phone's clock time). Which problems can occur?
questions.hint: What happens to the person whose phone clock is a few minutes ahead?

options.text: The one with the clock ahead keeps winning in the future, and other people's newer changes are silently dropped
options.why: The timestamp depends on the clock. Clock skew lets the wrong side win.

options.text: One of the two changes is lost without anyone knowing
options.why: LWW doesn't merge; it keeps one and throws the rest away.

options.text: When the line is back, both changes merge on their own
options.why: LWW doesn't merge. To merge you need a merge rule or a CRDT.

options.text: The system becomes CP at that point
options.why: Everyone is still getting answers, so it is still AP; it is just that the reconciliation rule is bad.
